issues.legal_issue: A later request to postpone performance, accepted by the promisee’s forbearance without a new performance date being fixed, makes a specific-performance claim subject to limitation running from notice of refusal rather than from the original performance date.
material_facts: The sale agreement made performance due after court restrictions on alienation were removed and the related proceedings terminated.
After the suits challenging the sale were dismissed, the sellers wrote that they intended to complete the sale but asked the purchasers to wait until matters became clearer before registration.
The purchasers accepted that request by not insisting on immediate performance or pursuing legal action.
The purchasers learned of the refusal to perform when they were forcibly dispossessed of the godown, and filed their specific-performance suit shortly afterward.
issues.conclusion: The later postponement, accepted by the purchasers’ forbearance, meant that no further date was fixed for performance; limitation therefore ran from the purchasers’ notice of refusal. The suit was within limitation and could not be dismissed as time-barred.
issues.legal_principle: Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides a three-year period for specific performance, running from the date fixed for performance or, if no date is fixed, from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused. Under Section 63 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a promisee may extend the time for performance; an extension need not be written and may be established by conduct, including forbearance. Applying Pazhaniappa Chettiyar v. South Indian Planting and Industrial Co. Ltd., an agreement initially having a fixed performance date may, in light of later events, become one with no date fixed. The Court treated Ramzan v. Hussaini and Tarlok Singh v. Vijay Kumar Sabharwal as binding on the general interpretation of Article 54, but found it unnecessary to resolve the broader question argued about that interpretation. Since the claim was timely, dismissal under Section 3 of the Limitation Act was not warranted.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and original_performance_date_fixed and sellers_requested_postponement_without_setting_new_date and purchaser_accepted_postponement_by_forbearance and purchaser_received_notice_of_refusal and suit_filed_within_three_years_after_notice

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.original_performance_date_fixed: The agreement initially made performance due upon the occurrence of a specified event.
predicates.sellers_requested_postponement_without_s: The sellers asked to delay performance but did not set a new date for it.
predicates.purchaser_accepted_postponement_by_forbe: The purchaser accepted the requested delay by refraining from insisting on immediate performance or pursuing legal action.
predicates.purchaser_received_notice_of_refusal: The purchaser learned that the sellers would not perform the agreement.
predicates.suit_filed_within_three_years_after_noti: The purchaser filed the specific-performance proceeding within three years after receiving notice of refusal.
predicates.suit_within_limitation: The specific-performance proceeding is within the applicable limitation period.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance claimant accepts the sellers’ request to postpone an initially scheduled performance without a new date by forbearing, and files within three years after learning of refusal, the proceeding is within limitation.
